newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan textiles soar as government plans relief.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan textiles soar as government plans relief.

text.p: Pakistani textile stocks have soared in the last two trading sessions in anticipation of a government relief package, but analysts said on Wednesday they saw no major turnaround in their earnings.

"There has been an unprecedented rise in textile stocks in the last two trading sessions on the news that the government plans a relief package. But people have over-reacted," ING Baring Securities analyst Amir Paracha said.

Baring's daily preview said the All Pakistan Textile Mills Association (APTMA) had urged the new caretaker government of Prime Minister Meraj Khalid to remove import charges on raw cotton and lower duties on the import of synthetic fibre.
Ather Rauf of Carr Mashriq said other demands of mill owners included a ban on cotton exports, rescheduling loan repayments by troubled textile companies and concessions on utilities.
"But most of these demands are economically unviable and if some are accepted, even then we do not see any turnaround in textile companies," he said.

Rauf said the government's textile reform package could be good for the economy as more than 60 percent of Pakistan's exports were cotton-based. "But we do not expect a turnaround in textile companies."
Abid Naqvi, research chief at Taurus Securities, said the government relief package would be in phases.
"Initially it will concentrate on the spinning sector and, with time, relief for value added sectors would be provided."
Dealers said one reform package could not pull the textile companies out of trouble while most of them had years of accumulated losses.

Naqvi said investors should take positions only in stocks with good track records and strong earning potential. "We recommend Gadoon Textiles and Nishat Mills which are trading at attractive earning levels," he said.

"The recovery of the textile sector will be a long process, another Taurus Securities dealer, Zaina Nowsherwan, said. "Most companies have five to six years of accumulated losses. They cannot bounce back in one year because of a single package."
